claims.claim: Switching on the thick filaments is faster than force development in amphibian muscle at 4°C.
claims.source: More generally, X-ray studies of the rising phase of the tetanus in amphibian muscle at 4°C showed that switching on the thick filaments is faster than force development (Reconditi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites published X-ray studies on thick filament activation kinetics.

claims.claim: Relaxation can be separated into a slow, almost linear phase ('isometric relaxation') followed by rapid 'chaotic relaxation' in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle.
claims.source: In isolated myofibrils and in single fibres from amphibian muscle, relaxation can be clearly separated into a slow, almost linear phase in which sarcomere lengths remain almost constant ('isometric relaxation') followed by mechanical yielding and rapid 'chaotic relaxation' in which the remaining force is rapidly lost (Brunello et al., 2009; Poggesi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites published work on the phases of muscle relaxation.

claims.claim: All measurements on mouse EDL muscle were made at 28°C.
claims.source: All of the present measurements on mouse EDL muscle were made at 28°C, a temperature at which the muscles contract reproducibly as required for signal averaging in X-ray experiments.
claims.evidence: The introduction explicitly states the experimental temperature.

claims.claim: The time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C.
claims.source: Moreover, the time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003), and the peak force is very close to that at the mammalian body temperature (Caremani et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites published characterization of calcium dynamics at the experimental temperature.

claims.claim: The peak force in mouse EDL at 28°C is very close to that at mammalian body temperature.
claims.source: Moreover, the time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003), and the peak force is very close to that at the mammalian body temperature (Caremani et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites published data on force production at different temperatures.

claims.claim: The off structure of the thick filament is preserved in mammalian muscle at 28°C.
claims.source: Most importantly, the off structure of the thick filament is preserved in mammalian muscle at this temperature (Caremani et al., 2021), in contrast with nearly all the published studies of thin filament regulation, for example, those using pCa titrations with steady-state Ca buffering in skinned muscle fibres, which were made at a relatively low temperature in order to minimise the irreversible effects of sustained high levels of activation at a high temperature.
claims.evidence: The introduction cites published work showing preservation of thick filament structure at the experimental temperature.

claims.claim: Five sarcomere reflections were observed, corresponding to even orders of the sarcomere repeat from the 10th to the 18th order in resting muscle.
claims.source: Five sarcomere reflections were observed, corresponding to even orders of the sarcomere repeat from the 10th to the 18th order in resting muscle (Figure 1A,B, cyan) (Bordas et al., 1987; Reconditi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed X-ray reflections with reference to the figure and citations.

claims.claim: Sarcomere length in the resting muscles was about 2.4 µm.
claims.source: Sarcomere length in the resting muscles was about 2.4 µm (Figure 1D; Table 1).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured sarcomere length with reference to figure and table.

claims.claim: Sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus.
claims.source: The sarcomere reflections became much weaker during stimulation, but sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus (Figure 1D, filled circles; Table 1), indicating that the sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle from which the X-ray signals were recorded had shortened by about 12%, presumably by stretching the tendons or compliant regions at the ends of the muscle fibres.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured sarcomere length during tetanus with reference to figure and table.

claims.claim: Sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle shortened by about 12% during tetanus.
claims.source: The sarcomere reflections became much weaker during stimulation, but sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus (Figure 1D, filled circles; Table 1), indicating that the sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle from which the X-ray signals were recorded had shortened by about 12%, presumably by stretching the tendons or compliant regions at the ends of the muscle fibres.
claims.evidence: The results section calculates the sarcomere shortening from the measured lengths.

claims.claim: Sarcomere length was maintained for about 20 ms after the last stimulus while force decreased to about 80% of its plateau value.
claims.source: This sarcomere length was maintained for about 20 ms after the last stimulus while force decreased to about 80% of its plateau value (Figure 1C,D, filled circles).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between sarcomere length and force during relaxation.

claims.claim: Relaxation of mouse EDL muscle from 100-ms tetani exhibits clear 'isometric' and 'chaotic' phases similar to those described previously in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle.
claims.source: Relaxation of mouse EDL muscle from 100-ms tetani, therefore, exhibits clear 'isometric' and 'chaotic' phases similar to those described previously in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle (Brunello et al., 2009; Poggesi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the observed relaxation phases to previously published findings.

claims.claim: There appeared to be little sarcomere shortening in the twitch.
claims.source: There appeared to be little sarcomere shortening in the twitch (Figure 1D, open circles), although the very low intensity of the sarcomere reflections (Figure 1E, open circles) suggests that sarcomere lengths became inhomogeneous, as during the first 20 ms of the tetanus.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the sarcomere behavior during twitch with reference to figures.

claims.claim: The (1,0) reflection became much weaker on activation in both the tetanus and the twitch, signalling motion of the myosin motors away from the thick filament backbone.
claims.source: The (1,0) reflection became much weaker on activation in both the tetanus (Figure 2A, orange) and the twitch (Figure 2B), signalling motion of the myosin motors away from the thick filament backbone (Haselgrove and Huxley, 1973).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed change in X-ray reflection with citation support for interpretation.

claims.claim: The (1,1) reflection became broader on activation and its integrated intensity increased, signalling increased mass at the trigonal positions of the filament lattice occupied by the thin filaments and increased disorder.
claims.source: The (1,1) reflection became broader on activation and its integrated intensity increased (Figure 2A,B, orange), signalling not only increased mass at the trigonal positions of the filament lattice occupied by the thin filaments, but also increased disorder.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed change in X-ray reflection and its structural interpretation.

claims.claim: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau.
claims.source: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau, similar to values reported previously for mouse EDL (Caremani et al., 2019), and ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured intensity ratios with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch.
claims.source: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau, similar to values reported previously for mouse EDL (Caremani et al., 2019), and ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured intensity ratio at twitch peak force.

claims.claim: The increase in I1,1/I1,0 was faster than force development at the start of the tetanus.
claims.source: The increase in I1,1/I1,0 was faster than force development at the start of the tetanus (Figure 2C, filled circles; Table 2), as observed in single fibres from amphibian fast skeletal muscle (Cecchi et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Myosin motors move towards the thin filaments before they bind strongly to actin or generate force.
claims.source: Since the fraction of myosin motors strongly attached to actin has the same time course as force (Brunello et al., 2006), the faster change in I1,1/I1,0 shows that myosin motors move towards the thin filaments before they bind strongly to actin or generate force.
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference from the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force with citation support.

claims.claim: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus with a time course similar to that of force development.
claims.source: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus (Figure 3C) with a time course similar to that of force development, but recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed change in actin layer line intensity and its temporal relationship to force.

claims.claim: IAL1 recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
claims.source: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus (Figure 3C) with a time course similar to that of force development, but recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor detachment from the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force.

claims.claim: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation with a time course much faster than that of force development.
claims.source: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation (Figure 3D) with a time course much faster than that of force development, showing that the loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin (Figure 3D; Table 2).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed change in myosin layer line intensity and draws an inference about motor conformation.

claims.claim: The loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin.
claims.source: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation (Figure 3D) with a time course much faster than that of force development, showing that the loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin (Figure 3D; Table 2).
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference about the sequence of structural changes from the temporal relationship between X-ray signals.

claims.claim: IML1 decreased almost as much at the peak of the twitch as at the plateau of the tetanus.
claims.source: Consistent with this faster response, IML1 decreased almost as much at the peak of the twitch (Figure 3D, open circles; Table 1) as at the plateau of the tetanus (filled circles).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the magnitude of IML1 decrease in twitch and tetanus.

claims.claim: IML1 did not recover during isometric relaxation after tetanic stimulation, consistent with myosin motors not reforming the folded helical conformation in this phase.
claims.source: IML1 did not recover during isometric relaxation after tetanic stimulation (Figure 3D, filled circles), consistent with the above conclusion that myosin motors do not reform the folded helical conformation in this phase, despite the fall of force and detachment of myosin motors from actin.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observed lack of IML1 recovery and draws an inference about motor conformation.

claims.claim: IML1 recovered rapidly but incompletely during chaotic relaxation; the 'off' conformation of the myosin motors had not been recovered even 120 ms after the last stimulus.
claims.source: IML1 recovered rapidly but incompletely during chaotic relaxation; the 'off' conformation of the myosin motors characteristic of the resting state had not been recovered even 120 ms after the last stimulus.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the incomplete recovery of IML1 during chaotic relaxation.

claims.claim: The M6 reflection is associated with a periodic structure in the thick filament backbone with an axial repeat of ~7.2 nm.
claims.source: The M6 reflection is associated with a periodic structure in the thick filament backbone with an axial repeat of ~7.2 nm (Reconditi et al., 2004; Huxley et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the structural origin of the M6 reflection with citation support.

claims.claim: SM6 increased by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus.
claims.source: The intensity of M6 reflection (IM6) was roughly constant during activation, within the reproducibility of the data (Figure 4C), but its spacing (SM6) increased consistently by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus (Figure 4D, filled circles; Table 1), and by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch (open circles).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M6 spacing during tetanus.

claims.claim: SM6 increased by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch.
claims.source: The intensity of M6 reflection (IM6) was roughly constant during activation, within the reproducibility of the data (Figure 4C), but its spacing (SM6) increased consistently by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus (Figure 4D, filled circles; Table 1), and by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch (open circles).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M6 spacing during twitch.

claims.claim: The spacing increase in SM6 is associated with activation of the thick filament.
claims.source: This spacing increase is associated with activation of the thick filament (Haselgrove, 1975).
claims.evidence: The results section cites published work linking SM6 spacing increase to thick filament activation.

claims.claim: SM6 increased much faster than force at the start of the tetanus.
claims.source: SM6 increased much faster than force at the start of the tetanus (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM6 and force development.

claims.claim: SM6 recovered with the same time course as force during isometric relaxation.
claims.source: Following the last stimulus, SM6 recovered with the same time course as force during isometric relaxation, but more slowly during chaotic relaxation (Figure 4D, filled circles).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM6 and force during relaxation.

claims.claim: SM6 recovery was still incomplete more than 120 ms after the last stimulus.
claims.source: SM6 recovery was still incomplete more than 120 ms after the last stimulus, and there was a smaller recovery deficit following a twitch.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the incomplete recovery of SM6 after tetanus.

claims.claim: The M3 reflection is associated with the axial periodicity of the myosin motors along the thick filaments.
claims.source: The M3 reflection is associated with the axial periodicity of the myosin motors along the thick filaments and has been used extensively to obtain information about the conformation and motion of myosin motors during activation, force generation, and relaxation (Brunello et al., 2009; Brunello et al., 2006; Reconditi et al., 2011; Reconditi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the structural origin of the M3 reflection with citation support.

claims.claim: IM3 decreased transiently in the tetanus before becoming about three times larger than at rest at the tetanus plateau.
claims.source: The intensity of the M3 reflection (IM3) decreased transiently in the tetanus before becoming about three times larger than at rest at the tetanus plateau (Figure 5C, filled circles; Table 1).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the biphasic change in IM3 during tetanus.

claims.claim: The initial decrease in IM3 may be partly due to the loss of some of the helically folded myosin motors and partly due to destructive interference between the actin-attached and folded populations of motors.
claims.source: The initial decrease may be partly due to the loss of some of the helically folded myosin motors that were present in the resting muscle and partly due to the destructive interference between the actin-attached and folded populations of motors (Reconditi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the initial IM3 decrease with citation support.

claims.claim: The slower increase in IM3 is associated with formation of actin-attached force-generating motors that have their long axes more perpendicular to the filament axis.
claims.source: The slower increase is associated with formation of actin-attached force-generating motors that have their long axes more perpendicular to the filament axis.
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the IM3 increase during tetanus.

claims.claim: IM3 only decreased in the twitch.
claims.source: IM3 only decreased in the twitch (open circles).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the different behavior of IM3 in twitch compared to tetanus.

claims.claim: SM3 increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau.
claims.source: The spacing of the M3 reflection (SM3) increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau and by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch (Figure 5D, Table 1), slightly smaller than the corresponding percentage increases in SM6 described above.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M3 spacing during tetanus.

claims.claim: SM3 increased by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch.
claims.source: The spacing of the M3 reflection (SM3) increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau and by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch (Figure 5D, Table 1), slightly smaller than the corresponding percentage increases in SM6 described above.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M3 spacing during twitch.

claims.claim: The increase in SM3 during the rising phase of the tetanus was faster than force but slower than SM6.
claims.source: The increase in SM3 during the rising phase of the tetanus was faster than force but slower than SM6 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM3, force, and SM6.

claims.claim: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation.
claims.source: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation (Figure 5D, filled circles), although IM3 recovered substantially towards its resting value (Figure 5C), indicating that the motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the behavior of SM3 during isometric relaxation and draws an inference about motor disorder.

claims.claim: The motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
claims.source: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation (Figure 5D, filled circles), although IM3 recovered substantially towards its resting value (Figure 5C), indicating that the motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor disorder from the different behaviors of SM3 and IM3.

claims.claim: SM3 decreased rapidly at the onset of chaotic relaxation and had completely recovered to its resting value at the end of mechanical relaxation.
claims.source: SM3 decreased rapidly at the onset of chaotic relaxation and had completely recovered to its resting value at the end of mechanical relaxation.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the recovery of SM3 during chaotic relaxation.

claims.claim: A new peak (the 'star' peak) appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the observation of a transient peak in the M3 reflection.

claims.claim: The star peak had a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured spacing of the star peak during tetanus.

claims.claim: The star peak had a spacing of 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the measured spacing of the star peak during twitch.

claims.claim: A peak with a similar spacing to the star peak was seen previously on cooling of resting EDL muscle of mice and demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle.
claims.source: A peak with a similar spacing was seen previously on cooling of resting EDL muscle of mice and demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle (Caremani et al., 2021; Caremani et al., 2019), an intervention that mimics activation of the thick filament.
claims.evidence: The results section cites previous observations of a similar peak under different conditions.

claims.claim: The best-fit model parameters were similar at rest and following mechanical relaxation after a twitch or tetanus.
claims.source: As expected from the similarity of the experimental M3 profiles, the best-fit model parameters were similar at rest and following mechanical relaxation after a twitch or tetanus (Figure 6B,E,G; Table 3).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the similarity of model parameters across different conditions.

claims.claim: At rest, nm was 2 and nd close to 46, indicating that nearly all 49 layers of myosin motors were ordered.
claims.source: nm was 2 and nd close to 46, indicating that nearly all 49 layers of myosin motors were ordered, with the likely exception of three layers at the filament tips.
claims.evidence: The results section interprets the model parameters in terms of the number of ordered motor layers.

claims.claim: At the tetanus plateau, all layers were ordered; nm was 1 and nd was 49.
claims.source: At the tetanus plateau (Figure 6F), all layers were ordered; nm was 1 and nd was 49.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the model parameters at tetanus plateau.

claims.claim: At the peak of the twitch, only myosin motors in a central region of each half-filament were ordered.
claims.source: nd was slightly smaller during early activation and at the peak of the twitch (Figure 6C,D), and nm was larger at the peak of the twitch, indicating that only myosin motors in a central region of each half-filament were ordered (Figure 6A), though that region did not correspond to either the conventional 'C-zone' defined by the presence of MyBP-C (green) or the 'C-type' titin repeats (magenta) (Bennett et al., 2020; Caremani et al., 2021; Tonino et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The results section interprets the model parameters at twitch peak force in terms of the spatial distribution of ordered motors.

claims.claim: The average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors away from the M line on activation was 11 nm.
claims.source: The average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors away from the M line on activation was 11 nm, the same as in the present experiments (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the calculated movement of motor center of mass.

claims.claim: There was no significant axial motion of the myosin heads during early activation.
claims.source: However, the best-fit hbz values in Table 3 also show that there was no significant axial motion of the myosin heads during early activation, reflecting the similarity of the intensity of the LA peak at this time point (Figure 5A,E, green; Figure 6C) to that at rest (Figure 5A,E, cyan; Figure 6B) and in marked contrast to the large reduction of the helical order of the myosin heads during early activation signalled by IML1 (Figure 3D, green).
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor motion from the model parameters and X-ray data.

claims.claim: The helical order is lost before myosin motors are released from the folded conformation on the filament backbone.
claims.source: Moreover, in the early activation time-frame, centred at 6.5 ms after the stimulus, IML1 had reduced by 50% (Figure 3D, green), but there was no axial movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors (hbz, Table 3), strongly suggesting that the helical order of the myosin motors is lost before their release from the folded conformation on the filament backbone.
claims.evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the sequence of structural changes from the X-ray data.

claims.claim: At the peak of the twitch, hbz had moved by about 6 nm, about half-way to its tetanus plateau value, suggesting that a significant fraction of motors remain in the folded state in the twitch.
claims.source: At the peak of the twitch, hbz had moved by about 6 nm, about half-way to its tetanus plateau value, suggesting that a significant fraction of motors remain in the folded state in the twitch.
claims.evidence: The results section draws an inference about the fraction of folded motors in the twitch from the model parameters.

claims.claim: The changes in thick filament structure during the tetanus can be correlated with force changes in five sequential phases: activation, tetanus plateau, isometric relaxation, chaotic relaxation, and mechanically relaxed.
claims.source: The functional significance of these structural changes is clearer for tetanus than for twitch, in which activation and relaxation are clearly separated by a period of steady-state sarcomere-isometric contraction in which the thin filaments are maximally activated by calcium. Changes in thick filament structure during the tetanus can be correlated with force changes in five sequential phases, which we refer to as activation, tetanus plateau, isometric relaxation, chaotic relaxation, and mechanically relaxed, where the latter is distinct from the resting state achieved several minutes after a previous contraction.
claims.evidence: The discussion section describes the framework for interpreting the structural changes.

claims.claim: The changes in the thick-filament-based X-ray reflections in the five phases are qualitatively similar to those described previously in fast-twitch amphibian muscles.
claims.source: Where analogous protocols have been employed, the changes in the thick-filament-based X-ray reflections in these five phases are qualitatively similar to those described previously in fast-twitch amphibian muscles, as described below.
claims.evidence: The discussion section compares the present findings to previous work on amphibian muscle.

claims.claim: The fastest changes in thick filament structure during activation are the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors and the elongation of the filament backbone.
claims.source: The fastest changes in thick filament structure during activation are the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors, signalled by the ML1 reflection, and the elongation of the filament backbone, signalled by SM6.
claims.evidence: The discussion section summarizes the fastest structural changes during activation.

claims.claim: The half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was about 8 ms.
claims.source: The fraction of molecules in a given conformation is proportional to the amplitude (A) of an X-ray reflection, the square root of its intensity. Therefore, the half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was estimated from the change in AML1, which has a half-time of about 8 ms, the same as that of SM6 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The discussion section reports the calculated half-time for loss of helical order.

claims.claim: The half-time of SM6 change during tetanus rise was about 8 ms.
claims.source: The fraction of molecules in a given conformation is proportional to the amplitude (A) of an X-ray reflection, the square root of its intensity. Therefore, the half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was estimated from the change in AML1, which has a half-time of about 8 ms, the same as that of SM6 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for SM6 change.

claims.claim: The equatorial intensity ratio (I1,1/I1,0), the fractional intensity of the LA peak of the M3 reflection (LM3), and the axial spacing of the myosin motors (SM3) have half-times of about 11 ms.
claims.source: A second group of signals, including the equatorial intensity ratio (I1,1/I1,0), the fractional intensity of the LA peak of the M3 reflection (LM3), and the axial spacing of the myosin motors (SM3), have half-times that are slightly slower, about 11 ms.
claims.evidence: The discussion section reports the half-times for a second group of structural signals.

claims.claim: The change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors.
claims.source: At the time resolution of these experiments, the change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors, whereas the axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
claims.evidence: The discussion section describes the temporal relationships between different structural changes.

claims.claim: The axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
claims.source: At the time resolution of these experiments, the change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors, whereas the axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
claims.evidence: The discussion section describes the temporal relationships between different structural changes.

claims.claim: The amplitude of the first actin layer line (AAL1) has a half-time of 15 ms, similar to that of force.
claims.source: The amplitude of the first actin layer line (AAL1), signalling myosin motor binding to the thin filaments, has a half-time of 15 ms, similar to that of force.
claims.evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for AAL1 change and compares it to force development.

claims.claim: AM3 has a half-time of 21 ms, slower than force.
claims.source: The only X-ray signal that is slower than force is AM3 (half-time, 21 ms), and this is likely related to its biphasic response (Figure 5C), with a fast decreasing phase followed by a slower rising phase.
claims.evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for AM3 change and provides an interpretation.

claims.claim: This sequence of structural changes during activation is similar to that reported for single fast-twitch fibres from frog skeletal muscle at 4°C, although all the changes are about three times faster in the conditions of the present experiments.
claims.source: This sequence of structural changes during activation is similar to that reported for single fast-twitch fibres from frog skeletal muscle at 4°C (Brunello et al., 2006; Piazzesi et al., 1999; Reconditi et al., 2011), although all the changes are about three times faster in the conditions of the present experiments.
claims.evidence: The discussion section compares the present findings to previous work on frog muscle.

claims.claim: The fastest structural changes in the thick filaments are slower than calcium activation of the thin filaments.
claims.source: The fastest structural changes in the thick filaments, those reported by AML1 and SM6, are slower than calcium activation of the thin filaments.
claims.evidence: The discussion section compares the kinetics of thick and thin filament activation.

claims.claim: The peak of the intracellular [Ca2+] transient is only 2.0 ms after the stimulus in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C.
claims.source: The peak of the intracellular [Ca2+] transient is only 2.0 ms after the stimulus in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C, and Ca2+ binding to troponin lags this by less than 1 ms (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
claims.evidence: The discussion section cites published data on calcium transient kinetics.

claims.claim: The rate of calcium-binding to troponin in response to a [Ca2+] jump is greater than 1000 s−1 at 12°C in demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle.
claims.source: Fluorescent probes on troponin in demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle showed that the rate of calcium-binding in response to a [Ca2+] jump is greater than 1000 s−1 at 12°C (Fusi et al., 2014b).

results.result: Time-resolved X-ray diffraction of isolated mouse EDL muscles at 28°C was used to characterize structural changes in thick filaments during muscle contraction. The experimental temperature preserves the thick filament 'off' state and allows reproducible contractions suitable for signal averaging, with calcium dynamics and force production well-characterized at this temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C21-C24 establish the experimental approach and justify the choice of 28°C as the experimental temperature. The cited literature (C22-C24) supports that calcium dynamics are characterized and thick filament structure is preserved at this temperature, providing a sound experimental foundation.

results.result: Sarcomere length measurements using ultra-low-angle X-ray diffraction revealed that sarcomeres shortened by ~12% during tetanus (from 2.4 to 2.13 µm) and remained isometric for ~20 ms after the last stimulus while force declined to 80% of plateau. Mouse EDL exhibits clear isometric and chaotic relaxation phases similar to amphibian muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 describe sarcomere length changes measured by X-ray diffraction with quantitative precision. The observation of isometric and chaotic relaxation phases (C29-C30) is well-supported by the data and comparison to previous work on amphibian muscle. The 12% sarcomere shortening (C28) is directly calculated from measured lengths.

results.result: Equatorial X-ray reflections show that myosin motors move radially toward thin filaments before strong actin binding or force generation. The intensity ratio I1,1/I1,0 increased from ~0.4 at rest to ~1.8 at tetanus plateau and ~0.9 at twitch peak, with kinetics faster than force development.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 describe equatorial reflection changes with quantitative measurements (C34-C35) and temporal relationships (C36). The inference that motors move toward thin filaments before strong binding (C37) is supported by comparison to cited work showing that strong attachment has the same time course as force (Brunello et al., 2006).

results.result: The first actin layer line (IAL1) increased threefold during tetanus with kinetics similar to force, while the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased much faster than force development. IML1 decreased similarly in twitch and tetanus but did not recover during isometric relaxation and recovered incompletely during chaotic relaxation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 describe layer line intensity changes with clear temporal relationships. The faster decrease of IML1 compared to force (C40-C41) and its incomplete recovery (C43-C44) are directly observed in the data. The inference that loss of helical conformation precedes actin attachment (C41) follows logically from the temporal data.

results.result: The M6 reflection spacing (SM6) increased by 1.54% during tetanus and 0.95% during twitch, signaling thick filament activation. SM6 increased faster than force at tetanus onset, recovered with force during isometric relaxation, but remained incompletely recovered >120 ms after the last stimulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 describe M6 reflection changes with precise quantitative measurements (C46-C47) and temporal relationships (C49-C51). The association with thick filament activation (C48) is supported by citation to Haselgrove, 1975. The incomplete recovery (C51) is directly observed.

results.result: The M3 reflection intensity (IM3) showed biphasic behavior during tetanus (initial decrease then threefold increase) but only decreased during twitch. M3 spacing (SM3) increased by 1.36% in tetanus and 0.57% in twitch, faster than force but slower than SM6. SM3 remained constant during isometric relaxation while IM3 recovered, indicating motor disorder.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C62 describe complex M3 reflection changes with quantitative measurements (C57-C58) and temporal relationships (C59). The inference that motors become disordered during isometric relaxation (C61) is logically derived from the different behaviors of SM3 and IM3 (C60). The biphasic IM3 response (C53-C55) is interpreted with citation support.

results.result: A transient 'star' peak appeared in the M3 reflection ~10 ms after stimulation onset with spacing of 14.832 nm during tetanus rise and 14.878 nm at twitch peak. A similar peak was previously observed upon cooling of resting muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 describe a novel observation with precise spacing measurements (C64-C65). The comparison to previous cooling experiments (C66) provides context, though the mechanistic interpretation remains incomplete. The observation itself is well-documented.

results.result: Modeling the M3 reflection axial profile showed that at rest nearly all 49 motor layers were ordered (nm=2, nd=46), while at tetanus plateau all layers were ordered (nm=1, nd=49). At twitch peak, only a central region was ordered (nm=9, nd=43). The motor center of mass moved 11 nm from rest to tetanus plateau, with no significant motion during early activation despite loss of helical order.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 describe modeling results with specific parameter values (C68-C70) and calculated motor movements (C71). The key inference that helical order is lost before motor unfolding (C73) is strongly supported by the observation that IML1 decreased 50% while hbz showed no change during early activation (C72). The 11 nm movement (C71) matches previous work on amphibian muscle.

results.result: During tetanus activation, structural changes occur in sequence with distinct kinetics: loss of helical order and backbone elongation are fastest (t1/2 ~8 ms), followed by motor radial motion and spacing changes (t1/2 ~11 ms), then actin attachment (t1/2 ~15 ms). This sequence is similar to amphibian muscle but ~3× faster.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C85 synthesize the temporal relationships between structural changes with quantitative half-times from Table 2 (C78-C84). The sequential nature of activation (C81-C82) is well-supported by the data. Comparison to amphibian muscle (C85) is appropriately cited. The framework of five phases (C75) provides clear organization.

results.result: Thick filament activation (t1/2 ~8 ms) is slower than thin filament activation (Ca2+ peak at 2 ms, troponin binding <1 ms, tropomyosin movement t1/2 <4 ms in amphibian muscle) but faster than actin attachment. This establishes thick filament activation as an intermediate regulatory step.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 establish the temporal hierarchy of activation steps by comparing thick filament kinetics to cited literature on thin filament activation (C87-C89). The conclusion that thick filament activation has two components intermediate between thin filament activation and actin attachment (C90) is well-supported. The mechanistic interpretation (C91) is appropriately cited.

results.result: At tetanus plateau, thin filaments are fully activated and ~30% of motors are strongly attached to actin. The 11 nm motor center of mass movement matches that in amphibian muscle, suggesting conserved motor conformations across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe the tetanus plateau state with appropriate citations for the fraction of attached motors (C92) and comparison to amphibian muscle (C93). The inference about conservation across species (C94) is reasonable given the structural similarities noted.

results.result: During isometric relaxation, sarcomeres remain isometric for ~20 ms while force decays to 80% of plateau. Motors detach from actin (signaled by decreasing I1,1/I1,0 and IAL1) but thick filament structure does not recover (IML1, SM3 constant), indicating a transient population of disordered motors.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C103 describe isometric relaxation with clear evidence from multiple X-ray signals (C99-C102). The inference about disordered motors (C103) logically follows from the delay between motor detachment and structural recovery. Comparison to previous work (C95-C97) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Motor detachment during relaxation has t1/2 ~23 ms (from AAL1) while helical order recovery has t1/2 ~42 ms (from AML1). At mechanical relaxation, motors had folded back (M3 profile recovered) but only ~80% regained helical packing (IML1 incomplete recovery). This incomplete recovery likely underlies post-tetanic potentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C111 describe relaxation kinetics with quantitative half-times and the key observation of incomplete helical recovery despite complete motor folding (C108-C109). The link to post-tetanic potentiation (C110-C111) is well-reasoned and cited. The mechanistic explanation (C111) follows logically.

results.result: Twitch peak force is ~25% of tetanus plateau force, primarily due to fewer actin-attached motors. Despite likely full troponin calcium occupancy (peak [Ca2+] similar in twitch and tetanus), thick filaments are incompletely activated with significant motors remaining folded, limiting force generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 establish the mechanism of low twitch force through multiple lines of evidence: quantitative force comparison (C112), X-ray evidence of fewer attached motors (C113), calcium data (C114-C115), and incomplete thick filament activation (C116-C117). The causal inference (C118) is well-supported.

results.result: Twitch duration is primarily determined by thin filament inactivation (Ca2+ transient t1/2 ~2 ms, troponin dissociation t1/2 ~25 ms at 28°C). Thick filament inactivation (IML1 t1/2 ~29 ms) is nearly synchronous with thin filament inactivation and force relaxation, contrasting with delayed thick filament inactivation after tetanus.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 establish the determinants of twitch duration through comparison of kinetics. The calcium data (C120-C121) combines cited literature with temperature extrapolation. The key finding of synchronous thick and thin filament inactivation in twitch (C123) contrasts clearly with tetanus behavior.

results.result: The twitch response is limited by incomplete thick filament activation despite transient complete thin filament activation. Motor attachment rate is partly limited by thick filament activation. This dual-filament regulatory framework extends previous thin filament-focused models.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 synthesize the major findings about twitch regulation. The conclusions about incomplete thick filament activation limiting force (C124) and attachment rate (C125) are well-supported by the data. The significance statement (C127) appropriately frames the contribution.

results.result: Physiological force generation in the twitch is limited by incomplete thick filament activation and rapid inactivation of both filaments. After tetanus, incomplete reformation of the helical array provides a structural basis for post-tetanic potentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 summarize major findings from the abstract. These are well-supported by the detailed results on twitch force limitation (C112-C126) and incomplete helical recovery after tetanus (C106-C111). The link to post-tetanic potentiation (C5) is mechanistically explained.
